body_markdown:
Almost one million Toyota Corollas have been sold every year since its debut in 1966.


In that time, there have been 12 generations and 57 million Corolla customers, with their cars being built in 14 factories across 11 countries. Quite simply, it’s the best-selling car on the planet.


A mover of the masses, the Corolla has also long been the choice of dedicated drivers, from the original drift king AE86 through World Rally success to the latest GR.


As the Corolla celebrates 60 years, let’s take a journey back to where it all began and how we got to this landmark moment.


## 1966


Toyota


The first Corolla was unveiled at the Tokyo auto show. The production version of a 1962 concept car, it was to be built at the new Takaoka plant in Toyota City. Chief engineer Tatsuo Hasegawa developed a true car of the people but didn’t cut corners in the process. The Corolla came with disc brakes, sports seats, multi-point seatbelts and two-speed wipers. Its 1.1-liter four-cylinder motor mustered 59 horsepower and drove the rear wheels via a four-speed manual transmission. Initially available as a two-door sedan, the range was expanded to include a four-door sedan, a wagon, and the Sprinter coupe. Named after the botanical term for the crown of petals in a flower, the Corolla soon became Toyota’s crown jewel. Within three years of going on sale in November 1966, it was Japan’s favorite car.


## 1970


Toyota


Corolla sales reached their first million just in time for the arrival of the second generation. Toyota revised the suspension and updated the interior to include such luxuries as seats with integrated headrests, an AM/FM radio, and windscreen washers. Air conditioning was even available. For enthusiasts, the arrival of the Levin fastback, with its 112-hp twin-overhead cam 1.6-liter engine, was even more exciting. In just four years, Toyota built 2.4 million second-gen Corollas, including the first to be assembled outside of Japan, thanks to a partner in Portugal.


## 1974


Toyota


Amid an oil crisis and tightened emissions rules, the third Corolla came boasting the Toyota Total Clean System, otherwise known as a catalytic converter. Also helping the updated model save fuel was a new wind-tunnel-tested design, with body styles now including a pillarless coupe, a hardtop, a semi-fastback, and a Liftback. It was the safest Corolla to date, with crumple zones and emergency locking seatbelts to protect occupants in the event of an accident. Buyers continued to flock to Toyota dealerships, and with 3.75 million examples sold, production had almost doubled again. Export markets were also booming, with annual sales abroad topping 300,000.


## 1979


Toyota


Another redesign, with a more slanted nose and a high rear deck, the fourth Corolla also brought rack-and-pinion steering and multilink rear suspension with coil springs to replace the earlier leaf springs. Diesel made its debut in the form of a 1.8-liter four-cylinder motor, which was frugal if not fast.


## 1983


Toyota


Drum roll, please. Corolla number five brought with it *the* fan favorite. While mainstream models made the switch to front-wheel drive, the AE86 coupe stuck with a rear-drive layout. In Japan, there were Levin and Trueno versions, while for Europe it came badged as the GT or GTi. The high-revving 1.6-liter double-overhead-cam four delivered more than 200 hp and a 0–60-mph time of eight seconds. For[touge tofu delivery drivers](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/this-1986-toyota-corolla-gt-s-ae86-turns-every-drive-into-a-tofu-run/) , a limited-slip differential was available. The *Hachi-Roku* (86) would become legend through *[Initial D](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/initial-d-at-30-a-historical-and-cultural-look-back/)* and inspire the entire[modern drift scene](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/drift-king-the-story-of-modern-motorsports-legend-keiichi-tsuchiya/) . As for the more conservative Corollas, they were styled for the first time using computer-aided design and gained features such as power steering, central locking, and electric windows.


## 1987


Toyota


All-wheel drive came to the Corolla in its sixth iteration. The entire range—which now included sedans, a coupe, hatchbacks, a wagon, and even a van—adopted a softer, wider-stance design. Front-drive was standard, but buyers could opt for extra traction, as well as a choice of six gasoline engines and one diesel, varying from around 60 hp to 140 hp.


## 1992


Toyota


The addition of the Lexus brand to the Toyota portfolio in 1989 also had benefits to the Corolla range. The seventh Corolla was bigger in every dimension, safer, faster, and quieter thanks to lessons learned from the luxury marque. The sedan was styled to look like a little LS400, panel gaps were tightened and bigger wheels fitted. A driver’s airbag came as standard, while a new move was to integrate the suspension and powertrain teams for a more cohesive drive to rival European marques.


## 1995


Toyota


Toyota’s one-size-fits-all approach ended with the eighth Corolla. The carmaker developed a unique model for Europe for the first time, where it was also built. High-tensile steel was used to increase rigidity and reduce weight for improved efficiency. Satellite navigation became an option, too. This was the model with which Toyota won the 1999 World Rally Championship, albeit a wild, all-wheel-drive, turbocharged, wide-bodied and be-winged version.


## 2000


Toyota


Toyota entered the 21st century with an all-new platform for the Corolla, known as the E120. The exterior design was again penned in Europe and targeted younger buyers, while the U.S. got a larger E130 version. Flush-fitting glass and aero-efficiency were key highlights, along with the Optitron instruments that first appeared in Lexus models. The Corolla Verso was introduced to add an MPV to the range, while Toyota’s variable valve timing technology, VVT-i, saw gasoline engines get a performance boost.


## 2007


Toyota


What were they thinking? The tenth-generation Corolla was not a Corolla at all. At least, not in Japan, Europe, or Australia, where, instead, it was named Auris. Revised multilink suspension was a feature, along with more airbags, electronic power steering, and a multi-mode auto transmission. It also became the first Corolla to be offered as a hybrid, with a Prius-style powertrain, and again the American edition was upsized compared to its European and Japanese counterparts.


## 2013


Toyota


Round 11 would see another complete redesign, but the Auris name stuck in most markets outside of the U.S. Toyota returned its focus to driver feedback, enhancing powertrains and suspension while reducing weight and honing aerodynamics. Once more, America got its own edition, which was larger, while the Euro version did also make it stateside with a bodykit and lowered suspension as the Scion iM (later Corolla iM).


## 2019


Toyota


Toyota finally saw the error of its ways, and the Corolla name returned to the world. Newly developed on the Toyota New Global Architecture platform, improvements included a lower center of gravity and better body rigidity. A choice of hybrid powertrains was offered, and the Gazoo Racing team also got hold of the Corolla, creating the wild 300-hp GR Corolla, an absolute weapon for road and track and the most potent Corolla ever.


The 13th-generation Corolla is due out in 2028. What’s in store is anybody’s guess, but the next car could be offered with a few different powertrains, including hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and fully electric options. Will an ICE-only option make the cut? We’ll know soon enough.
